subject: Architecture
title: Timbuktu: Mud Mosques of the Sahel
description: A fast breakdown of Timbuktu: Mud Mosques of the Sahel for builders.

hook.text: Timbuktu's mosques are built from mud bricks and look like nothing else in the world.

buildup.text: The Great Mosque of Djenné is the largest mud-brick building on Earth — rebuilt annually by the community.

discovery.text: Wooden beams called 'toron' stick out from the walls — they serve as permanent scaffolding for repairs.

twist.text: Every year, the entire city holds a festival to replaster the mosque. It takes 4,000 workers one day.

climax.text: Mud architecture is perfectly adapted to the Sahel climate — thick walls insulate against extreme heat.

punchline.text: The biggest mud building on Earth. Replastered by hand every year.

quiz.question: What are the 'toron' beams sticking out of Djenné's mosque?
options: Permanent scaffolding for annual maintenance and repair
Structural supports to prevent wall collapse

details.summary: Timbuktu's mosques, including the Great Mosque of Djenné, are built from sun-dried mud brick reinforced with wooden scaffolding beams called torons. These adobe structures require annual communal replastering, making their maintenance a living cultural tradition rather than simple preservation.
details.whyItMatters: Mud brick architecture demonstrates that monumental buildings don't require stone or concrete. The annual replastering tradition keeps construction knowledge alive across generations, making the building itself a cultural practice.
takeaways: Mosques are built from sun-dried mud brick with wooden torons
Annual communal replastering maintains both structure and culture
Mud architecture achieved monumental scale without stone or metal

faq.question: Why is the annual replastering important?
faq.answer: Rain erodes mud brick surfaces every season. The communal replastering festival involves the entire community working together, passing down construction techniques through participation. This living tradition is as important as the physical building it maintains.

faq.question: Is the Great Mosque of Djenné really the largest mud building?
faq.answer: Yes. The current structure, rebuilt in 1907 following the original design, is the world's largest mud-brick building. It measures roughly 75 by 75 meters and can hold 3,000 worshippers. UNESCO designated it a World Heritage Site in 1988.
